h1: What an SEO agency is (and what it isn't)
metaTitle: What Is an SEO Agency? A Plain Definition
metaDescription: What is an SEO agency? A team you rent to grow organic search traffic. The plain definition, the four models it gets confused with, and its real limits.
answer: An SEO agency is a team you rent to grow the traffic your website earns from search. Typically five to fifteen people covering technical, content, links and analytics, on a monthly retainer of ₹25,000–₹3,00,000. Unlike a freelancer it covers all four disciplines at once; unlike an in-house hire, it leaves when you stop paying.
takeaways: An SEO agency is **rented capacity across four disciplines** — technical, content, links, analytics. That breadth is the entire product. One specialist with a company name is a freelancer.
In India a real boutique runs **5–15 people**; a mid-size shop 30–80. Below five you're buying a freelancer collective, which can be excellent — just price it that way.
One word covers four different businesses: agency, freelancer, in-house team, white-label reseller. Three of them will happily call themselves the first one.
An agency doesn't control Google, doesn't fix your pricing, and usually doesn't ship your code. Knowing that before you sign saves you a year.

body: An SEO agency is a company you pay monthly to increase the traffic and revenue your website earns from unpaid search results. It supplies people rather than software: strategists, technical specialists, writers, editors, outreach staff and analysts, pointed at your site instead of you hiring them yourself.

That's the whole idea. You're renting a bench you couldn't justify building. One in-house SEO hire in India typically costs ₹6–18 lakh a year and gives you a single skill set. An agency retainer at ₹75,000/month costs roughly ₹9 lakh a year and gives you four skill sets, part-time. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on how much of each skill you actually need.

One thing worth knowing up front: the word "agency" has no gatekeeping attached to it. No certification, no licence, no register. One person with a laptop and a payment link can call themselves an SEO agency, and thousands do. So the definition that matters isn't the dictionary one — it's the operational one below.

callout.title: The short version
callout.body: An agency is a team you rent. If what you're being sold is one person's time, it's a freelancer. If it's a dashboard, it's software. Both can be good buys. Neither is an agency.

sections.h2: Agency, freelancer, in-house, reseller — four businesses, one word
body: Most confusion about SEO agencies is really confusion between four different ways of buying the same work. Each has a different headcount, a different cost profile, and its own way of failing.

table.caption: How the four models compare in the Indian market. Ranges are typical, not fixed.
head: Model
Who you actually get

callout.title: The question that separates them
callout.body: "Is any part of this work subcontracted, and to whom?" A clean answer is fine — plenty of good agencies outsource writing or outreach and say so. A vague one means you've found the reseller.

subs.h3: Why the reseller row matters most
body: The reseller is the model that most often calls itself an agency, because the front end is identical: a website, a deck, a monthly report. The difference is that the person selling you the work isn't doing it, and frequently doesn't know who is. If you want the cost maths in full, [agency versus freelancer](/compare/agency-vs-freelancer) and [agency versus in-house](/compare/agency-vs-in-house) work through it properly.
A working SEO agency needs five functions covered. At a small shop, one person covers two of them. At a large one, each is a department.
bullets: **Strategist / account lead** — owns the plan and the number you're measured on. The one name you should know.
**Technical SEO** — crawling, indexing, page speed, schema, redirects, migrations.
**Content** — keyword research, briefs, writing, editing. Usually the largest group by headcount.
**Links / digital PR** — outreach, data stories, placements. The function most often quietly outsourced.
**Analytics** — tracking setup, dashboards, attribution. The function most often quietly skipped.

subs.h3: The number that tells you more than headcount
body: A five-person agency has genuine specialists in two of those five functions and generalists doing the rest, which is fine if your bottleneck happens to be one of the two. A sixty-person agency has all five, and a much higher chance you're handed to whoever had capacity that month.

So the useful question isn't total headcount — it's **accounts per strategist**. Somewhere around six to eight clients per strategist, the plan stops being written for you and starts being a template with your logo on it. We cap ourselves at three new clients a month for exactly that reason.

sections.h2: What an SEO agency does not do
body: Half the disappointment in this market comes from work the client assumed was included. It usually isn't, and some of it can't be.
bullets: **It doesn't control Google.** No agency has a lever on the index. Anyone promising a specific position for a specific keyword is describing something they cannot deliver.

**It usually doesn't ship your code.** Most agencies write the ticket; your developer merges it. Confirm who deploys before month one — an unshipped fix list is the commonest reason a technical audit produces nothing.
**It doesn't fix your offer.** If your pricing, product or sales follow-up is the problem, more organic traffic just gives you a larger sample of people who don't buy.
**It doesn't normally include paid media.** SEO and Google Ads are separate line items run by separate people, even inside the same company.
**It doesn't include design, hosting or translation** unless the contract names them. Read [what SEO services include](/answers/what-do-seo-services-include) before assuming.
**It can't rescue an unknown site in 90 days.** It can start. Three to six months is the honest floor for a competitive keyword set, and anyone quoting less is quoting a smaller problem than yours.

sections.h2: SEO agency vs digital marketing agency
body: A digital marketing agency sells the whole channel mix — paid search, paid social, organic social, email, sometimes creative and web build. An SEO agency sells one channel and goes considerably deeper into it.

The trade cuts both ways. A generalist gives you one contract, one invoice and one meeting; you'll usually get a competent-but-shallow SEO practice inside it, because SEO is the least profitable service in the mix and the easiest to under-resource without anyone noticing for six months. A specialist gives you depth and a team that will argue with you about canonical tags; you'll be the one coordinating them with whoever runs your ads.

Rough rule: if organic search is a supporting channel and paid is your engine, a generalist is fine. If organic search is the channel your business plan depends on, buy the specialist. If you're not sure which you are, look at where your qualified leads actually came from last quarter — that's the answer, not the ambition. For what the broader label covers, see [what a digital marketing agency is](/answers/what-is-a-digital-marketing-agency).

sections.h2: Six questions that reveal which one you're talking to
body: You can identify the model in about four minutes if you ask these in order and watch the pauses rather than the answers.
numbered: **Who runs my account day to day, and what else are they on?** You want a name and a number. Hesitation here is the single most informative moment in any agency meeting.
**Is any of this subcontracted?** Writing and outreach often are, legitimately. You want to know, not to be protected from knowing.
**Where do your links come from?** "Our network" means a private blog network. That's a penalty with a date on it you haven't been told.
**What number are we measuring, and what is it today?** If nobody writes down the starting point, nobody can prove movement later — which suits one party more than the other.
**Who ships the technical fixes — you or my developer?** Get it in writing. It decides whether the audit becomes work or a PDF.

**What happens if it doesn't work?** Most answers are a shrug dressed up as process. Ours: we freeze your trailing-90-day qualified organic leads on day one, and if we haven't beaten that number in 90 days we keep working free until we do.

faqs.q: Is an SEO agency worth it for a small business?
faqs.a: It depends on whether your competition is doing SEO. A single-location service business with three local rivals can often get most of the value from a well-run Google Business Profile and a fast site. Once you're competing nationally, or against anyone publishing weekly, the four-discipline breadth an agency provides starts to matter.

faqs.q: How big is a typical SEO agency?
faqs.a: Indian boutiques usually run 5–15 people; mid-size shops 30–80. What matters more is the pod on your account — typically three to six people — and how many other clients that pod carries. Past roughly six to eight accounts per strategist, your plan is a template.

faqs.q: What's the difference between an SEO agency and an SEO consultant?
faqs.a: A consultant sells judgement and a plan; an agency sells judgement plus the hands to execute it. Consultants suit companies with an in-house team that needs direction. Agencies suit companies with no in-house SEO capability at all. Paying an agency for advice you then can't implement is the common expensive mistake.

faqs.q: Do SEO agencies work with every industry?
faqs.a: Most will take anything, which isn't a compliment. Industry knowledge genuinely matters in regulated categories — healthcare, finance, legal — where content has compliance constraints and E-E-A-T signals carry real weight. Ask to see work in a category with similar constraints, not necessarily your exact vertical.

faqs.q: How much does an SEO agency cost in India?
faqs.a: Retainers run roughly ₹25,000 to ₹3,00,000 a month. Below ₹25,000 you're funding part-time freelancer attention, whatever the invoice says. ₹75,000–₹1,50,000 is where a multi-discipline team becomes viable for a competitive national keyword set. Ours starts at ₹75,000/mo, with smaller sites from ₹40,000.
